modern_osis:
Lamentations — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Henry considers Jeremiah to be the clear author of the Lamentations traditionally associated with his name.

He dates the book after the Chaldeans destroyed Jerusalem.

May it teach us to recognize sin as the cause of our calamities, and amid trials to practice submission, repentance, faith and prayer, trusting in the promised deliverance that comes through God's mercy.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins.1–11Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God.12–22
Jerusalem's desolation follows her sins (verses 1–11)

At times the prophet speaks in his own person.

At other times Jerusalem is personified as a distressed woman, or the words are spoken by some of the Jews.

The lament portrays the Jewish nation's misery.

Because of the greatness of her sins, Jerusalem had become a captive and a slave.

She found no rest from suffering.

If we permit sin, our greatest enemy, to govern us, we should not be astonished when other enemies are also allowed to rule over us.

The people experienced the extremes of famine and distress.

In these terrible circumstances Jerusalem acknowledged her sins and asked the Lord to consider her suffering.

This is the only way to find rest under such burdens.

God's just anger against human transgression has filled the world with sorrow, lamentation, sickness and death.

Jerusalem mourns and seeks mercy (verses 12–22)

Jerusalem is pictured sitting in grief upon the ground.

She asks everyone passing by to consider whether her example should concern them.

Her outward suffering was great, but the guilt she felt made her inward suffering even harder to bear.

True sorrow over sin must reach the depths of the soul.

This scene shows sin's dreadful character and calls us to flee from coming judgment.

Yet however much we may learn from Jerusalem's suffering, we can learn far more from the suffering of Christ.

Does he not address every one of us from the cross?

“Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?”

May all our sorrows lead us to Christ's cross, teach us to attend to his example and enable us to follow him willingly and joyfully.
classic_reading:
[Lam.1.1-Lam.1.11]
Lamentations
It is evident that Jeremiah was the author of the Lamentations which bear his name. The book was not written till after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. May we be led to consider sin as the cause of all our calamities, and under trials exercise submission, repentance, faith, and prayer, with the hope of promised deliverance through God's mercy.
Chapter 1
The miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins. ( [Lam.1.1-Lam.1.11] La 1:1-11) Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God. ( [Lam.1.12-Lam.1.22] La 1:12-22)
Verses 1-11 The prophet sometimes speaks in his own person; at other times Jerusalem, as a distressed female, is the speaker, or some of the Jews. The description shows the miseries of the Jewish nation. Jerusalem became a captive and a slave, by reason of the greatness of her sins; and had no rest from suffering. If we allow sin, our greatest adversary, to have dominion over us, justly will other enemies also be suffered to have dominion. The people endured the extremities of famine and distress. In this sad condition Jerusalem acknowledged her sin, and entreated the Lord to look upon her case. This is the only way to make ourselves easy under our burdens; for it is the just anger of the Lord for man's transgressions, that has filled the earth with sorrows, lamentations, sickness, and death.
[Lam.1.12-Lam.1.22]
Verses 12-22 Jerusalem, sitting dejected on the ground, calls on those that passed by, to consider whether her example did not concern them. Her outward sufferings were great, but her inward sufferings were harder to bear, through the sense of guilt. Sorrow for sin must be great sorrow, and must affect the soul. Here we see the evil of sin, and may take warning to flee from the wrath to come. Whatever may be learned from the sufferings of Jerusalem, far more may be learned from the sufferings of Christ. Does he not from the cross speak to every one of us? Does he not say, Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? Let all our sorrows lead us to the cross of Christ, lead us to mark his example, and cheerfully to follow him.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem.

God withdraws protection from Jerusalem (verses 1–9)

The passage gives a sorrowful picture of God's church, Jacob and Israel.

It particularly directs attention to the Lord's hand in the people's suffering.

Yet God does not become an enemy of his people simply because he is angry with them and corrects them.

When he withdraws protection, city gates and iron bars can provide no security.

It is right for God to humble people through judgment when they have degraded themselves through sin.

Those who fail to value or observe his Sabbaths and appointed worship may justly lose the comfort and benefit of them.

What use do people make of Bibles if they refuse to learn from them?

Those who misuse God's prophets may rightly lose them.

It can be painful to direct suffering people's attention to their own wrongdoing and God's judgment.

Nevertheless, that recognition may be necessary because their sins are the source of their miseries.

The terrible suffering and a call to prayer (verses 10–22)

There were many reasons for mourning.

Countless people died through famine.

Even children were killed by their mothers and eaten, in fulfillment of the dreadful warning of Deuteronomy 28:53.

Many more died by the sword.

False prophets deceived the people.

Their neighbors mocked them.

Mocking another person's suffering is a serious sin and adds to that suffering.

Their enemies celebrated their defeat.

Yet those hostile to God's church often mistake its severe setbacks for its final destruction.

They will discover their error.

The suffering people are called to lament, and to seek comfort for their grief.

Prayer is a remedy for every wound, even the deepest and most painful.

In prayer we bring our circumstances to the Lord and entrust them to him.

May his will be done.

Let us fear God, walk humbly before him and take care that we do not fall.
classic_reading:
[Lam.2.1-Lam.2.9]
Chapter 2
Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem.
Verses 1-9 A sad representation is here made of the state of God's church, of Jacob and Israel; but the notice seems mostly to refer to the hand of the Lord in their calamities. Yet God is not an enemy to his people, when he is angry with them and corrects them. And gates and bars stand in no stead when God withdraws his protection. It is just with God to cast down those by judgments, who debase themselves by sin; and to deprive those of the benefit and comfort of sabbaths and ordinances, who have not duly valued nor observed them. What should they do with Bibles, who make no improvement of them? Those who misuse God's prophets, justly lose them. It becomes necessary, though painful, to turn the thoughts of the afflicted to the hand of God lifted up against them, and to their sins as the source of their miseries.
[Lam.2.10-Lam.2.22]
Verses 10-22 Causes for lamentation are described. Multitudes perished by famine. Even little children were slain by their mother's hands, and eaten, according to the threatening, Deut. 28:53. Multitudes fell by the sword. Their false prophets deceived them. And their neighbours laughed at them. It is a great sin to jest at others' miseries, and adds much affliction to the afflicted. Their enemies triumphed over them. The enemies of the church are apt to take its shocks for its ruins; but they will find themselves deceived. Calls to lamentation are given; and comforts for the cure of these lamentations are sought. Prayer is a salve for every sore, even the sorest; a remedy for every malady, even the most grievous. Our business in prayer is to refer our case to the Lord, and leave it with him. His will be done. Let us fear God, and walk humbly before him, and take heed lest we fall.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies.

The prophet's grief and temptation (verses 1–20)

The prophet describes the darkest and most discouraging part of his experience before explaining where he found help and relief.

During his trial, the Lord seemed terrifying to him.

His affliction felt like misery itself, because sin makes suffering's cup bitter.

The struggle between unbelief and faith may become very severe.

Yet even the weakest believer is mistaken when imagining that strength and hope from the Lord have entirely disappeared.

The Lord's mercies are new every morning (verses 21–36)

Having described his distress and temptations, the prophet now shows how he rose above them.

However bad our condition is, God's mercy is the reason it is not worse.

We should notice not only what works against us, but also the gifts and promises that support us.

God's compassion never fails.

Every morning provides fresh evidence of it.

Earthly possessions and inheritances perish, but the Lord himself is a portion forever.

It is our duty, and also our comfort, to hope and wait quietly for his salvation.

Afflictions may accomplish much good.

Many have found that bearing the yoke in youth makes them serious, humble and less attached to the world, when otherwise they might have been proud and unruly.

When suffering produces patience, patience can deepen experience, and that experience strengthens a hope that does not put us to shame.

Remembering both sin's evil and our own sinfulness shows us that we are not consumed only because of the Lord's mercies.

Perhaps we cannot yet say with steady confidence, “The Lord is my portion.”

But can we not at least pray, “I desire him as my portion and salvation; I hope in his word”?

Happy are those who learn to receive their affliction as being under God's sovereign hand.

Examine your own ways and return to God (verses 37–41)

As long as life remains, hope remains.

Rather than only complaining that things are bad, we should encourage ourselves that they may become better.

Our sins deserve far more suffering than we actually receive.

We should bring our complaint to God, not complain against God.

During disaster we are quick to examine other people's ways and blame them.

But our duty is to search and test our own ways, and turn away from sin toward God.

Our hearts must accompany our prayers.

If inward conviction does not correspond to outward words, we mock God and deceive ourselves.

The prophet weeps and waits for God (verses 42–54)

The more the prophet contemplated the devastation, the more deeply he grieved.

Yet one word of comfort remained.

While the people continued weeping, they also continued waiting.

They looked to the Lord alone for relief and rescue.

Faith finds courage in God's answer (verses 55–66)

Faith finally emerges victorious.

The prophet ends with a measure of comfort.

Prayer is the breath of a person made new by God.

In asking for mercy, the renewed soul draws in grace like air.

In praise, that soul breathes it back.

Prayer reveals spiritual life and helps sustain it.

God calmed the people's fears and quieted their hearts.

He said, “Do not fear.”

That was the language of his grace, borne witness by his Spirit to their spirits.

And what are our sufferings compared with the sufferings of the Redeemer?

The Lord will deliver his people from their troubles and renew his church after persecution.

He will save believers with everlasting salvation, while his enemies face eternal judgment.
classic_reading:
[Lam.3.1-Lam.3.20]
Chapter 3
The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies.
Verses 1-20 The prophet relates the more gloomy and discouraging part of his experience, and how he found support and relief. In the time of his trial the Lord had become terrible to him. It was an affliction that was misery itself; for sin makes the cup of affliction a bitter cup. The struggle between unbelief and faith is often very severe. But the weakest believer is wrong, if he thinks that his strength and hope are perished from the Lord.
[Lam.3.21-Lam.3.36]
Verses 21-36 Having stated his distress and temptation, the prophet shows how he was raised above it. Bad as things are, it is owing to the mercy of God that they are not worse. We should observe what makes for us, as well as what is against us. God's compassions fail not; of this we have fresh instances every morning. Portions on earth are perishing things, but God is a portion for ever. It is our duty, and will be our comfort and satisfaction, to hope and quietly to wait for the salvation of the Lord. Afflictions do and will work very much for good: many have found it good to bear this yoke in their youth; it has made many humble and serious, and has weaned them from the world, who otherwise would have been proud and unruly. If tribulation work patience, that patience will work experience, and that experience a hope that makes not ashamed. Due thoughts of the evil of sin, and of our own sinfulness, will convince us that it is of the Lord's mercies we are not consumed. If we cannot say with unwavering voice, The Lord is my portion; may we not say, I desire to have Him for my portion and salvation, and in his word do I hope? Happy shall we be, if we learn to receive affliction as laid upon us by the hand of God.
[Lam.3.37-Lam.3.41]
Verses 37-41 While there is life there is hope; and instead of complaining that things are bad, we should encourage ourselves with the hope they will be better. We are sinful men, and what we complain of, is far less than our sins deserve. We should complain to God, and not of him. We are apt, in times of calamity, to reflect on other people's ways, and blame them; but our duty is to search and try our own ways, that we may turn from evil to God. Our hearts must go with our prayers. If inward impressions do not answer to outward expressions, we mock God, and deceive ourselves.
[Lam.3.42-Lam.3.54]
Verses 42-54 The more the prophet looked on the desolations, the more he was grieved. Here is one word of comfort. While they continued weeping, they continued waiting; and neither did nor would expect relief and succour from any but the Lord.
[Lam.3.55-Lam.3.66]
Verses 55-66 Faith comes off conqueror, for in these verses the prophet concludes with some comfort. Prayer is the breath of the new man, drawing in the air of mercy in petitions, and returning it in praises; it proves and maintains the spiritual life. He silenced their fears, and quieted their spirits. Thou saidst, Fear not. This was the language of God's grace, by the witness of his Spirit with their spirits. And what are all our sorrows, compared with those of the Redeemer? He will deliver his people from every trouble, and revive his church from every persecution. He will save believers with everlasting salvation, while his enemies perish with everlasting destruction.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity.

Jerusalem's former beauty is lost (verses 1–12)

What a change has taken place!

Sin dims the beauty of even the noblest abilities and the most excellent gifts.

But the gold that Christ bestows and has tested in the fire can never be taken away.

Its outward appearance may lose its shine, but its true value never changes.

Once more we hear of the horrors of Jerusalem's siege and destruction.

As we consider what sin brought upon God's people in earlier times, we should think seriously about what the same causes might bring upon the church today.

Lord, though we have rebelled against you, turn to us and turn our hearts back to you.

Help us to fear your name.

Bless us with grace that awakens, converts, renews and strengthens.

The sins of leaders hasten the nation's ruin (verses 13–20)

Nothing brings a people toward ruin more quickly than the sins of their priests and prophets.

Even the king could not escape, for God's justice pursued him.

Yet our anointed King alone is the life of our souls.

We may dwell safely under Christ's shadow and rejoice in him even among enemies.

He is the true God and eternal life.

Zion's suffering will end; Edom faces judgment (verses 21 and 22)

The prophecy announces that Zion's troubles will reach an end.

It does not mean that she will suffer the complete punishment she deserved, but that she will experience everything God has determined to inflict.

Edom's celebration will also end.

The troubles of God's church and each believer will soon be completed.

The judgment of their enemies is drawing near.

The Lord will expose their sins, and they will lie down in lasting sorrow.

In Henry's interpretation, Edom here represents all the church's enemies.

The prophet has shown how widespread Israel's corruption was.

That reality demonstrates God's justice in the judgments he sent.

It also reveals how urgently the whole human race needs the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Lam.4.1-Lam.4.12]
Chapter 4
The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity.
Verses 1-12 What a change is here! Sin tarnishes the beauty of the most exalted powers and the most excellent gifts; but that gold, tried in the fire, which Christ bestows, never will be taken from us; its outward appearance may be dimmed, but its real value can never be changed. The horrors of the siege and destruction of Jerusalem are again described. Beholding the sad consequences of sin in the church of old, let us seriously consider to what the same causes may justly bring down the church now. But, Lord, though we have gone from thee in rebellion, yet turn to us, and turn our hearts to thee, that we may fear thy name. Come to us, bless us with awakening, converting, renewing, confirming grace.
[Lam.4.13-Lam.4.20]
Verses 13-20 Nothing ripens a people more for ruin, nor fills the measure faster, than the sins of priests and prophets. The king himself cannot escape, for Divine vengeance pursues him. Our anointed King alone is the life of our souls; we may safely live under his shadow, and rejoice in Him in the midst of our enemies, for He is the true God and eternal life.
[Lam.4.21-Lam.4.22]
Verse 21 ,22 Here it is foretold that an end should be put to Zion's troubles. Not the fulness of punishment deserved, but of what God has determined to inflict. An end shall be put to Edom's triumphs. All the troubles of the church and of the believer will soon be accomplished. And the doom of their enemies approaches. The Lord will bring their sins to light, and they shall lie down in eternal sorrow. Edom here represents all the enemies of the church. And the corruption, and sin of Israel, which the prophet has proved to be universal, justifies the judgments of the Lord. It shows the need of that grace in Christ Jesus, which the sin and corruption of all mankind make so necessary.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour.

The people confess their sufferings and sins (verses 1–16)

Is anyone suffering?

Let that person pray, bringing the complaint directly to God.

That is what God's people do here.

They lament not merely dangers they imagine, but hardships they are already enduring.

When we experience suffering connected with the sins of our ancestors, we may hope in the Lord's returning mercy if we remain repentant and patient.

The people confess: “Woe to us, for we have sinned!”

Our sorrow is ultimately tied to our own sin and folly.

Although our sins and God's righteous displeasure cause suffering, we may hope for his forgiving mercy, sanctifying grace and kind Providence.

Yet the guilt accumulated through a lifetime of sin will finally be judged unless a person receives an interest in the Savior who bore our sins in his own body on the tree.

The people pray for renewed favor (verses 17–22)

The devastation of the temple concerned God's people even more deeply than all their other troubles.

But despite every change on earth, God remains the same.

He is forever wise and holy, just and good.

With him there is no variation or shadow of change.

The people pray earnestly for mercy and grace:

“Turn us to you, O Lord.”

God never abandons people before they abandon him.

If his grace brings them back to himself in obedience, he will show them favor and mercy.

If he renews our hearts, he will also renew our days through his kindness.

Troubles may weaken our hearts and dim our eyes, but the throne of mercy of our reconciled God remains open.

In every trial, let us place our entire trust in his mercy, confess our sins and pour out our hearts before him.

Guard against resentment and despair.

All who trust, fear, love and serve the Lord will find that all is well in the end.

God's judgments still occur in the earth, as in Jeremiah's time.

Let us therefore remember Zion in our prayers and seek her welfare above every earthly joy.

Spare your people, Lord, and do not allow your heritage to become a reproach under the power of other nations.
classic_reading:
[Lam.5.1-Lam.5.16]
Chapter 5
The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour.
Verses 1-16 Is any afflicted? Let him pray; and let him in prayer pour out his complaint to God. The people of God do so here; they complain not of evils feared, but of evils felt. If penitent and patient under what we suffer for the sins of our fathers, we may expect that He who punishes, will return in mercy to us. They acknowledge, Woe unto us that we have sinned! All our woes are owing to our own sin and folly. Though our sins and God's just displeasure cause our sufferings, we may hope in his pardoning mercy, his sanctifying grace, and his kind providence. But the sins of a man's whole life will be punished with vengeance at last, unless he obtains an interest in Him who bare our sins in his own body on the tree.
[Lam.5.17-Lam.5.22]
Verses 17-22 The people of God express deep concern for the ruins of the temple, more than for any other of their calamities. But whatever changes there are on earth, God is still the same, and remains for ever wise and holy, just and good; with Him there is no variableness nor shadow of turning. They earnestly pray to God for mercy and grace; Turn us to thee, O Lord. God never leaves any till they first leave him; if he turns them to him in a way of duty, no doubt he will quickly return to them in a way of mercy. If God by his grace renew our hearts, he will by his favour renew our days. Troubles may cause our hearts to be faint, and our eyes to be dim, but the way to the mercy-seat of our reconciled God is open. Let us, in all our trials, put our whole trust and confidence in his mercy; let us confess our sins, and pour out our hearts before him. Let us watch against repinings and despondency; for we surely know, that it shall be well in the end with all that trust in, fear, love, and serve the Lord. Are not the Lord's judgments in the earth the same as in Jeremiah's days? Let Zion then be remembered by us in our prayers, and her welfare be sought above every earthly joy. Spare, Lord, spare thy people, and give not thine heritage to reproach, for the heathen to rule over them.
